title_eng: The Optimal Attachment Position for a Fingertip Photoplethysmographic Sensor With Low DC
abstract:
IEEE SENSORS JOURNAL, VOL. 12, NO. 5, MA Y 2012 1253
The Optimal Attachment Position for a Fingertip
Photoplethysmographic Sensor With Low DC
Chungkeun Lee, Hang Sik Shin , Student Member , IEEE, Jongchul Park, and Myoungho Lee
Abstract— In this study, optimal position was approached by a
search of a low-DC drift sensor attachment position for measuring
photoplethysmography. DC and AC models were proposed by
merging the Lambert–Beer equations at the conventional PPG
onset and the peak into one equation. The position at which point
the DC ﬂuctuation is small and the AC component is large in the
PPG was suggested. Among the lateral sides of four blood vessels,
the dorsal, palmer, ulnar, and radial vessels region, the ulnar vessel
region showed small DC amplitude and the largest AC amplitude
and perfusion index.
Index T erms— Nonpulsatile component (DC), optimal position,
perfusion index, photoplethysmography (PPG), pulsatile compo-
nent (AC).
I. I NTRODUCTION
P
HOTOPLETHYSMOGRAPHY (PPG) is used in various
ways in the mobile healthcare system, including cardio-
vascular monitoring as its measurement technique is simple
and because it allows noninvasive cardiovascular assessment
[1], [2]. The PPG signals are composed of AC components and
DC components; the AC components are related to the blood
volume of the pulsatile component in the artery synchronized
with the heartbeat, and the DC components are related to the
venous blood volume and the nonpulsatile component in the
artery. The DC components are removed to measure the AC
waveforms with a high signal-to-noise ratio in most commercial
products and related studies [1]. Given that the DC components
can vary drastically due to respiration and cold stress [3], DC
removal with a conventional hardware ﬁlter or the digital ﬁlters
such as ﬁnite impulse response (FIR) and Inﬁnite impulse
response (IIR) is limited [4]. Thus, a high system load and cost
are required for DC component removal from the real-time mo-
bile PPG system. In this study, we propose the optimal position
at which the DC amplitude is small and the AC component is
large for a real-time mobile PPG system.

C. Experiment and Signal Processing
A total of ten healthy subjects (10 males, age 29.8
 2.6)
who consented to the experimental objective and progress par-
ticipated in the experiment. In the experiment, the ECG, PPG,
respiration, and skin temperature were measured for 1 min. All
of the signals were measured at a 1 kHz sampling rate using the
ECG100C, PPG100C, RSP100C, and SKT100C measurements
of a BIOPAC system (BIOPAC System Inc., U.S.). The position
of radial and ulnar vessels on distal is at lower right and left of
the ﬁnger bone [8]. As shown in Fig. 1, the PPG signal was mea-
sured in the palmer, ulnar, radial, and dorsal directions using a
TSD200 within the 0.05
 10 Hz, amplifying the signals con-
stantly by 20 times. The respiration was measured to observe
the drastic change of the AC and DC components by deep in-
spiration using the TSD201C sensor [3]. The distal temperature
affects the transcutaneous blood ﬂow [3], it was measured to
check whether or not a constant temperature was maintained.
We selected the PPG duration where there was an ECG beat
without drastic AC and DC variation upon deep respiration and
temperature. The AC components were obtained using a 0.5 Hz
FIR high-pass ﬁlter, and the DC components were obtained
using a 0.5 Hz low-pass ﬁlter. The RMS (root-mean-square) of
the AC and DC components was then calculated. The PI was
also calculated to monitor the characteristics of perfusion ac-
cording to the positions. All signal processing was performed
using MA TLAB (Mathworks, Natick, MA, U.S.). For the sta-
tistical test, a Wilcoxon signed rank test was carried out using
SPSS (SPSS-IBM Inc., Chicago, IL, U.S.), and a

The size and the distribution of the arteries and veins found
in physiological reports [8], [9] were fairly consistent with the
results of this study. The ulnar has the largest arterial vessel and
the smallest vein count. The PI was largest at the ulnar region,
while it was smallest at the dorsal side. The ulnar region showed
a relatively high DC component when compared to the other re-
gions except the palmer region, which may have arisen because
the nonpulsatile component was greater in the artery.
Therefore, we think that it is needed to investigate distribution
of artery and vein at measurement position for a remote sensing
of PPG using webcam or smartphone-camera.
